name: service-oriented-architecture
context: Enterprise integration architecture using services as interoperable building blocks connected via a central Enterprise Service Bus (ESB), enabling heterogeneous systems to communicate through standardized contracts and enterprise integration patterns.
benefits: Enterprise-wide interoperability through standardized service contracts
Legacy system integration by wrapping existing systems as services
Business capability reuse across multiple applications
Vendor independence via open standards (SOAP, WSDL, UDDI)
tradeoffs: ESB becomes single point of failure and potential bottleneck
Vendor lock-in with ESB products (IBM, Oracle, TIBCO)
use_cases: Integrating multiple enterprise systems (ERP, CRM, SCM)
avoid_when: Team autonomy is prioritized over governance
component_types: Enterprise Service Bus (ESB): Central hub for service communication and routing
Service Registry: Repository for service metadata enabling discovery
Service Repository: Store for service artifacts, contracts, and documentation
Business Process Engine (BPM): Orchestrates services into business processes
Message Router: Routes messages based on content or routing rules
Protocol Mediator: Translates between different protocols
Policy Manager: Enforces governance and security policies
SLA Manager: Monitors and enforces service level agreements
Audit Logger: Tracks service interactions for compliance
Data Transformer: Transforms data formats between services
anti_patterns: God service (monolithic service doing too much)
ESB as data store (storing state in the bus)
best_practices: Establish Governance Early: Create architectural review board and service governance before building services
Start Incrementally: Begin with pilot project, prove value, then expand enterprise-wide
Design for Reuse: Target services at enterprise-wide capabilities, not department-specific needs
Use Canonical Protocols: Standardize on common protocols (SOAP/REST) across all services
Implement Service Registry: Maintain centralized registry for service discovery and documentation
Monitor ESB Health: Central bus monitoring is critical: ESB health determines system reliability
Plan for Versioning: Design services to support multiple versions coexisting
Wrap Legacy Systems: Integrate existing systems as services rather than replacing them
Document Service Contracts: Provide clear ICD (Interface Control Document) for each service
Enforce Security Boundaries: Implement authentication and authorization at service level
